notes.tech: Thread proposed 4 (2026-10-11): Chrome-R; D.D. Shell; Flatt; Gore G-Type; Metro-Tek; MetroShell; MetroShield; Micro Kei — house-named fabrics (Chrome-R, Shell-R, D.D. Shell, Nycra-R, Flatt Nylon, Micro Kei, Metro-Tek, Micro-Tek) plus licensed PrimaLoft® and GORE-TEX (Gore G-Type); share of range 45/212 styles name one of these fabrics in title or composition. Seated as proposed, pending ruling.
notes.craft: Thread proposed 3 (2026-10-11): C.P. documents its signature process (garment dyeing) in detail and publishes a passport with the weaving, dyeing and sewing country for nearly every product. It names no factory or mill and owns no facility on the evidence read, so 3 rests on process and supply-chain disclosure rather than named making. Seated as proposed, pending ruling.

craft_evidence.mills: no: fabrics carry house names, mills not named
craft_evidence.madein: 193/212 styles state a confection country in the product passport (weaving and dyeing countries alongside)
craft_evidence.heritage: dated and placed: "In 1971, Osti founded Chester Perry ... In 1978, Chester Perry became C.P. Company" in Bologna (/en-us/our-story.html)
craft_evidence.process: yes: garment dyeing explained step by step against piece dyeing, with the 1970s origin and the 2005 first garment-dyed GORE-TEX (/en-us/garment-dyeing.html); product passport gives the weaving, dyeing and confection country for each product
craft_evidence.reasoning: C.P. documents its signature process (garment dyeing) in detail and publishes a passport with the weaving, dyeing and sewing country for nearly every product. It names no factory or mill and owns no facility on the evidence read, so 3 rests on process and supply-chain disclosure rather than named making.
